subject: technology
topic: A glowing screen before bed pushes your body clock later
angle: While screen time is linked to poorer sleep outcomes and shorter sleep duration in infants, toddlers, and preschoolers, meta-analysis did not confirm these unfavorable associations in preschoolers.
title: The Screen and the Sleep Cycle

hooks.text: Does a screen change how a child sleeps?
You assume screens hurt every child's sleep. The evidence is mixed.
You use a screen to soothe a restless child.
A blue light glows in a dark nursery.

reveal.headline: The evidence for preschooler sleep disruption is mixed.
reveal.body: While screen time is linked to poorer sleep outcomes in infants and toddlers, meta-analysis did not confirm these unfavorable associations in preschoolers.

explain.headline: Screen time affects young children differently.
explain.body: Excessive screen time is linked to shorter sleep duration in toddlers and preschoolers. It is also linked to disrupted sleep across these age groups.

matters.headline: Age changes the impact of the screen.
matters.body: The strength and consistency of the link between screens and sleep vary by age group. That may be why the impact is not uniform for every child.

example.headline: A toddler watches a tablet in a dim room.
example.body: The light from the screen reflects on their face as they sit on the rug. They do not move. The room is quiet except for the sound of the video.

question.headline: Does the screen dictate the rhythm of your home?

claims.text: Meta-analysis confirmed these unfavorable associations in infants and toddlers but not preschoolers.
claims.quote: Meta-analysis confirmed these unfavorable associations in infants and toddlers but not preschoolers.

claims.text: Screen time is linked to poorer sleep outcomes in infants, toddlers and preschoolers.
claims.quote: Results indicate that screen time is associated with poorer sleep outcomes in infants, toddlers and preschoolers.

claims.text: Excessive screen time is linked to shorter sleep duration among toddlers and preschoolers.
claims.quote: Strong evidence of the meta-analysis suggested that excessive screen time was associated with overweight/obesity and shorter sleep duration among toddlers and preschoolers.

claims.text: Excessive screen time is linked to disrupted sleep.
claims.quote: Excessive screen time ([Formula: see text] 2 h per day) is associated with childhood overweight and obesity, physical inactivity, increased sedentary time, unfavorable dietary behaviors, and disrupted sleep.

claims.text: Sleep latency, percentages of stage 1 and stage 2 significantly increased with age in adults.
claims.quote: In adults, it appeared that sleep latency, percentages of stage 1 and stage 2 significantly increased with age while percentage of REM sleep decreased.

verdict: The evidence shows a link between screen time and poorer sleep in young children, but the strength and consistency of this association vary by age group.
caveat: The overall quality of evidence for these associations in children under 5 was reported as very low.
caption:
Screen time and sleep are linked in young children.

Research shows these links are established for infants and toddlers but not confirmed for preschoolers.

How do you balance screen time in your household?
